title: Quantifying soil moisture and evapotranspiration heterogeneity within a solar farm: Implications for stormwater management
abstract: As solar energy becomes a cheap source of renewable energy, the number of major utility-scale ground solar panel installations, often called ‘solar farms,’ are growing. With these solar farms often covering hundreds of acres, there is potential for impacts on natural hydrologic processes, including runoff generation and erosion. There is still limited research in this area, and best management practices to address these impacts are variable and not well understood. To fill this gap, we conducted a field investigation of soil moisture patterns, solar radiation, and vegetation at two solar farms in central Pennsylvania, USA that are representative of the complex terrain in the region (e.g., high or variable slopes). Both solar farms also included engineered infiltration basins or trenches that were investigated. Analysis of soil moisture patterns reveals redistribution of water relative to panels, with dripline soil moisture 19 % higher than the reference, and underpanel moisture 25 % lower than the reference, on average at both solar farms over a year. There are also the greatest periods of saturation and runoff generation at the panel driplines. However, an open interspace between panel rows and existing infiltration basins and trenches are playing a critical role in managing runoff. Micrometeorological monitoring indicates reduced evapotranspiration (ET) under panels, with potential underpanel ET 37–67 % lower in summer, and minimal difference in winter. However, a survey of vegetation revealed almost complete ground coverage under panels, which is critical for supporting infiltration and reducing erosion. As solar farms expand to meet important renewable energy goals, it is essential that care be taken to design the landscape to minimize runoff generation and erosion. This work demonstrates that healthy vegetation and well-draining soils can help manage runoff on solar farms; where necessary on more challenging landscapes, engineered stormwater controls can manage any unmitigated runoff.

- 22 **Highlights:**

- 23 • 20-29% lower soil moisture and 60-88% lower solar radiation occurred under panels.

- 24 • There is increased soil moisture and incidence of saturation at the dripline.

- 25 • Differences in ET and soil moisture within the solar farm vary by season.

- 26 • The interspace zone facilitates infiltration, leading to reduced incidence of saturation.

- 27 • Stormwater management strategies can manage changes in runoff from solar farms.

## 29 **Abstract**

30

- 31 As solar energy becomes a cheap source of renewable energy, the number of major utility-scale 32 ground solar panel installations, often called ‘solar farms,’ are growing. With these solar farms 33 often covering hundreds of acres, there is potential for impacts on natural hydrologic processes, 34 including runoff generation and erosion. There is still limited research in this area, and best 35 management practices to address these impacts are variable and not well understood. To fill this 36 gap, we conducted a field investigation of soil moisture patterns, solar radiation, and vegetation 37 at two solar farms in central Pennsylvania, USA that are representative of the complex terrain in 38 the region (e.g., high or variable slopes). Both solar farms also included engineered infiltration 39 basins or trenches that were investigated. Analysis of soil moisture patterns reveals redistribution 40 of water relative to panels, with dripline soil moisture 19% higher than the reference, and 41 underpanel moisture 25% lower than the reference, on average at both solar farms over a year. 42 There are also the greatest periods of saturation and runoff generation at the panel driplines. 43 However, an open interspace between panel rows and existing infiltration basins and trenches are 44 playing a critical role in managing runoff. Micrometeorological monitoring indicates reduced 45 evapotranspiration (ET) under panels, with potential underpanel ET 37-67% lower in summer, 46 and minimal difference in winter. However, a survey of vegetation revealed almost complete 47 ground coverage under panels, which is critical for supporting infiltration and reducing erosion. 48 As solar farms expand to meet important renewable energy goals, it is essential that care be taken 49 to design the landscape to minimize runoff generation and erosion.  This work demonstrates that 50 healthy vegetation and well-draining soils can help manage runoff on solar farms; where 51 necessary on more challenging landscapes, engineered stormwater controls can manage any 52 unmitigated runoff.

53

- 54 **1. Introduction**

- 55 1.1.The expansion of solar farms

- 56 Technologies to harvest solar energy have rapidly expanded in recent decades due to technological 57 advancements and favorable government policies that make it more affordable, along with goals 58 for reducing the carbon footprint of energy (Gunerhan et al., 2008; Shorabeh et al., 2019). Ground 59 mounted solar arrays are one of the methods used for harnessing solar energy. Utility- scale 60 ground-mounted solar arrays generating at least 1 MW of electricity are commonly referred to as 61 ‘solar farms’. As of 2023, there are approximately 6,440 existing major solar projects across the 62 US, with existing installations generating 104 GW, and projects under construction or in 63 development generating 111 GW (Solar Energy Industries Association, 2023). The area covered 64 by solar farms can vary between 1 acre (0.40 ha) to hundreds of acres (Aman et al., 2015; Jacobson 65 & Delucchi, 2011). Historically, many of these projects were developed in areas most abundant in 66 solar radiation. However, there is increasing development of solar energy infrastructure across a 67 variety of landscapes and climatic regions (US Energy Information Administration (EIA), 2023).

- 68 Solar farms present a unique land use transition, where impervious solar panels are mounted on 69 metal supports above pervious land. There is the potential for negative impacts on the environment, 70 depending on the way that the solar farm is built and maintained (Hernandez et al., 2014). For 71 example, vegetation type and management and solar panel height and spacing could all impact the 72 ecosystem functions on a solar farm (Yavari et al., 2022). With respect to hydrology, there is the 73 potential for impacts to hydrologic processes, as panels intercept precipitation and route it to a 74 concentrated drip zone, as well as intercept solar radiation, which is a major influence on 75 evapotranspiration. However, there is very limited existing research characterizing how solar 76 farms may change environmental characteristics and function.

- 77 1.2. Existing research on solar farm hydrology and soils

- 78 1.2.1. Soil physical properties and soil moisture

- 79 Field measurements on solar farms have often been made at specific locations relative to solar 80 panels- these have included the interspace area open to sun between panels, under the lower edge 81 of the panel or ‘dripline’, and underneath the center of the panels. Sometimes measurements may 82 also be made at a control or reference area outside the main array of panels.

- 83

- 84 Physical, chemical, and biological soil indicators have been found to be lower or unchanged on 85 solar farms compared to reference land cover types. No change in bulk density has been observed 86 at multiple solar farms (Armstrong et al., 2016; Lambert et al., 2021). Reductions in soil carbon 87 and nitrogen content have been documented (Choi et al., 2020; Lambert et al., 2021), in addition 88 to lack of difference in soil nutrients (Choi et al., 2023). There is also evidence of the impacts of 89 land management choices; no significant changes in soil physical and chemical properties were 90 observed at a solar farm on reclaimed cropland sown with meadow grasses (Armstrong et al., 91 2016).

- 92

- 93 Some soil properties may also vary within the solar farm. Hydraulic conductivity was found to be 94 higher beneath solar panels than in the interspace area between panels. The reason for this 95 difference may be the reduced exposure to maintenance activities beneath the panel, which could 96 induce compaction and reduce hydraulic conductivity (Choi et al., 2020).

- 97

- 98 Substantial variation in soil moisture has also been observed within solar farms. In multiple solar 99 farms, particularly those in more arid environments, relatively higher moisture has been observed

- 100 under panels (Barron-Gafford et al., 2019; Hassanpour Adeh et al., 2018; Yue et al., 2021). These 101 patterns are presumably driven by reduced evapotranspiration (ET). At multiple sites, the dripline 102 has had relatively higher soil moisture compared to the reference, under panel, or interspace, 103 particularly following rain events (Choi et al., 2020, 2023; Yassin Elamri et al., 2018; McCall et 104 al., 2023).

- 105 1.2.2. Micro-meteorology and evapotranspiration

- 106 The presence of solar panels can alter meteorological characteristics. Because they may interrupt 107 the movement of air, reduced wind speed and altered wind direction has been observed under solar 108 panels (Choi et al., 2023; Hassanpour Adeh et al., 2018).  Solar panels can also impact the balance 109 of incoming solar radiation and emitted radiation, in turn altering soil temperature and ET.

- 110 Reduced solar radiation has been consistently observed under solar panels (Armstrong et al., 2016; 111 Hassanpour Adeh et al., 2018; Kannenberg et al., 2023; Marrou, Guilioni, et al., 2013). Changes 112 in these variables also manifest in changes in ET, where reductions in ET have been observed 113 under panels in multiple solar farms (Y. Elamri et al., 2018; Marrou, Dufour, et al., 2013). 114 However, recent work has demonstrated that these ET reductions can be much less than solar 115 radiation reductions under the panels, thanks to strategic changes in photosynthetic traits by plants 116 (Kannenberg et al., 2023).

- 117 1.2.3 Runoff

- 118 The soil and hydrologic variables discussed above have implications for runoff generation, but 119 there has been almost no direct study of runoff on solar farms. Two recent plot-scale field studies 120 have investigated runoff from ground-mounted solar panels. While one study found no measurable 121 impact on runoff volume or velocity from solar panels over bare soil as compared to bare soil alone 122 (Wang & Gao, 2023), the second study observed increased peak discharge (Baiamonte, Gristina, 123 & Palermo, 2023). Because these studies did not compare other land covers, it is unclear how 124 addition of solar panels may affect vegetated landscapes. Increased roughness under the panels did 125 lead to reduced sediment fluxes compared to the control (Wang & Gao, 2023) but it is important 126 to again note that this was without the presence of vegetation. Because this study did not compare 127 other land covers, it is unclear how addition of solar panels may affect other soils or vegetated 128 landscapes. Several published modeling studies have evaluated the impacts of solar farms on 129 runoff. Their results have varied from no net impact on runoff to net increases in runoff from solar 130 farms, as compared to pre-development conditions (Cook & McCuen, 2013; Edalat, 2017; Gullotta 131 et al., 2023; McCall et al., 2023; Nair et al., 2023; Pisinaras et al., 2014). However, most hydrologic 132 modeling approaches for solar farms did not explicitly represent the impervious solar panels over 133 pervious land, and thus the results may not reflect reality. Recently, EPA Stormwater Management 134 Model (SWMM) and Hydrus have been used to represent solar farm runoff generation, in a way 135 where there is both the impervious surface of the panel, and underlying pervious surface (Gullotta 136 et al., 2023; McCall et al., 2023; Nair et al., 2023). The two SWMM modeling studies found that 137 solar farms had minimal impact on runoff for smaller storm events, but could increase runoff 138 volume and peak flow for larger storm events (Gullotta et al., 2023; Nair et al., 2023).

- 139 1.3 Objectives of this study

- 140 As the rapid development of solar farms continues to meet renewable energy goals, it is critical 141 that we understand their potential impacts on landscape hydrology, and how to best manage and 142 minimize these impacts. It is important to understand how redistribution of soil moisture may 143 manifest in changes in runoff generation.

- 144 In this research, we focus on the hydrological impacts of solar farms by quantifying various 145 hydrologic parameters including soil moisture, runoff, and evapotranspiration. We specifically 146 focus on two solar farms that have more complex terrain than those previously investigated, 147 specifically higher slopes. These two solar farms have many similar characteristics (e.g. soil type, 148 slope magnitude, managed meadow vegetation); despite these similarities, the ability to study two 149 sites allows consideration of inevitable heterogeneities of natural landscapes.

- 150 The first objective is to understand how solar farm implementation in a humid continental climate 151 changes soil moisture patterns and resulting potential for runoff generation. We hypothesize that 152 the under panel area does not receive direct precipitation, and thus we expect it to be driest. 153 However, the dripline receives runoff from the solar panel surface; therefore, higher soil moisture 154 and incidence of saturation is expected at the dripline. Our second objective is to understand the

- 155 performance of stormwater management strategies on these solar farms, including impervious

- 156 disconnection and structural stormwater management (e.g. infiltration trenches). By characterizing 157 changes in soil moisture and the potential for resulting runoff generation, as well as understanding 158 whether existing stormwater management strategies are able to manage generated runoff, we can 159 support the sustainable development of solar farms on more marginal landscapes.

- 160 **2 Materials and Methods**

- 161 2.1 Solar farm research sites

- 162 The two solar farm research sites are located in the State College area in central Pennsylvania, 163 USA. This region is at the edge of the ridge and valley landscape and is characterized by variable 164 topography and karst geology.  The average annual temperature in State College is 9.3 °C. Annual 165 average rainfall is 1088 mm (Climate Data for Cities Worldwide (CDCW), 2023).

166

167

168

169

170 Figure 1: Map of two studied solar farms with location of sensors, including solar farm 2 (top left) and solar farm 1 171 (bottom). At the top right, the location of these sites within Pennsylvania USA is indicated.

172

- 173 Solar farm 1 is located adjacent to Penn State University- University Park campus (Figure 1; Figure 174 2a). It was developed in 2019, generates 2 MW, and covers 2.6 ha. The pre-development conditions 175 in this site were a combination of mostly meadow and pasture. The soil type is mapped as 176 Opequon-Hagerstown complex, which is predominantly silty clay loam. The solar farm has a 177 consistent slope of about 25% directed down towards an adjacent road. The solar panels are 178 oriented in the same direction as the land slope. There are three linear infiltration basins at the base 179 of the slope (Figure 2c). The basins vary in length based on the width of the upslope solar panel 180 rows, but the basin that was instrumented is 75 m. Each basin is approximately 1 m depth. These 181 basins were designed on the basis of Pennsylvania’s solar-specific stormwater management 182 guidance, which requires more detailed consideration of runoff calculations when the slope is 183 greater than 10% (Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (PA DEP), 2021). In this 184 case, runoff calculations were based on a modified Curve Number to factor in the potential effect 185 of solar panels, where stormwater design targets were no net increase in runoff volume for a 2 186 year-24 hour event, and no net increase in peak flows for a 100 year event (Minnesota Pollution

- 187 Control Agency, 2019). During solar farm development, the site was seeded with a low-growth 188 native perennial seed mixture. Mowing is conducted several times per year.

- 189

- 190 Solar farm 2 is located at a wastewater treatment authority to the northeast of State College, PA 191 and covers a total of 7 ha (Figure 1). Soils at this site are Hagerstown silt loam or Opequon192 Hagerstown complex, primarily silty clay loam. There are also small sections of rock outcrops. 193 The solar farm was constructed over multiple years, where Phase 1 was constructed in 2018 and 194 produces 2.6 MW of electricity, and Phase 2 was completed in spring 2021 and produces 3.5 MW 195 of electricity. Slopes at the solar farm are variable, ranging from a few percent to over 30%. Due 196 to the local township stormwater ordinance, Phase 2 has gravel infiltration trenches that are 197 implemented along the topographic contours of the landscape (Figure 2b). Each trench is 30 cm 198 wide, 20 cm deep, and filled to the surface with gravel. The entire site was grazed by sheep starting 199 in June 2022. Field measurements were made in multiple areas of the farm, with a cluster of soil 200 moisture sensors located around a row on the north side/ phase 1, and an infiltration trench 201 monitored on the south part of the solar farm. Figure 2d shows the location of the sensors around 202 the panels.

203

204 The width of panels in both solar farms is 4 m. The width of the interspace zone between the panels 205 at both sites is 3 m. The vertical height of the lower edge of the panel is 1.5 m in solar farm 1. In 206 solar farm 2 the vertical height of the lower panel edge varies between 0.8 to 1.5 m. At both sites, 207 panels are fixed tilt, and are mounted towards the south at approximately a 40 degree angle, given 208 the location in central Pennsylvania.

209

- 211 Figure 2: Photos and Schematic of the solar farms: (a) solar farm 1 (steep site); (b) solar farm 2 with infiltration trench; 212 (c) infiltration basin at base of solar farm 1, and (d) schematic of key monitoring locations relative to solar panels

- 213 2.2 Continuous measurements

- 214 2.2.1 Soil moisture

- 215 To investigate the effects of solar panels on the soil moisture distribution around the panels, we 216 implemented several clusters of soil moisture sensors at depth of 10cm at different locations 217 relative to the panels (Figure 2d). These clusters were located away from the edges of the solar 218 farm to be as representative as possible. Three METER TEROS 12 sensors were implemented 219 around the panels during summer and fall 2021 at the following locations: interspace, under panel 220 and dripline. Each detects volumetric water content (VWC; vol/vol). We implemented one cluster 221 of sensors around one of the panel rows in solar farm 1, and one sensor at the reference point off 222 to the side of the row where other sensors were implemented (Figure 1). The sensor implemented 223 in the reference site is not affected by the panels (there is not any panel upslope of the reference 224 point). Each sensor records VWC, temperature, and soil electrical conductivity at 15-minute 225 intervals. The data is recorded automatically with the installed METER ZL6 data loggers. We also 226 added one cluster of sensors around a panel row in solar farm 2; also at solar farm 2, we added 227 TEROS 12 sensors on either side of an infiltration trench. In addition to using soil moisture 228 timeseries to evaluate changes in time and space, we also leveraged this data to evaluate patterns 229 of saturation (i.e., plateau at a maximum value for a given location), and presumed runoff 230 generation.

- 231 2.2.2. Meteorology and ET

- 232 Meteorological data is available for both solar farms. For solar farm 1, a weather station was 233 already located nearby (~ 2 km) to the solar farm. The HOBO RX3000 weather station logs data 234 on rainfall, air temperature, wind speed, solar radiation, humidity, and barometric pressure at 5- 235 minute intervals. At solar farm 2, a METER ATMOS 41 weather station was installed at the site, 236 several meters away from any panels. This station collects the same variables as solar farm 1, at 237 15-minute intervals. To compare the solar radiation under the solar panels with the reference 238 points, we installed additional pyranometers (METER PYR). The pyranometers were located at 239 the underpanel location at solar farm 1 and solar farm 2.

- 240 We assessed daily potential evapotranspiration beneath solar panels in comparison to the reference 241 point (not affected by solar panels). For underpanel ET computations, we utilized the same dataset 242 collected from the weather stations, with the sole exception being solar radiation; in this case, data 243 from the underpanel pyranometers was used. Potential ET was then calculated for both under panel 244 and reference point conditions at each solar farm using the Penman-Monteith method, facilitated 245 by the ‘evapotranspiration’ R package (Guo et al., 2016).

- 246 2.2.3 Runoff

- 247 To measure the runoff that reaches the base of the slope at solar farm 1, we installed three Onset 248 HOBO U20L water level loggers along the infiltration basin of the selected watershed. Three

- 249 loggers were installed, given the length of the infiltration basin (Figure 1), to capture any 250 heterogeneity in runoff or the basin; ultimately the middle logger is used for presented data analysis

- 251 in this paper. Water level data was logged at 5-minute intervals between fall 2021 and summer 252 2023; however, the loggers were removed during winter periods, and data was not available for 253 other selected periods of time for other reasons.

- 254 2.3 Manual field measurements

- 255 Soil hydraulic conductivity was measured using a METER SATURO infiltrometer at multiple sites 256 in each solar farm. In addition, soil samples were taken in close proximity to the soil moisture 257 sensor clusters using a bulk density corer as well as a cylindrical push probe for a 10 cm deep 258 sample; two soil samples for all analyses were taken at each sensor location and properties of the 259 two samples were averaged. Samples were analyzed for bulk density, soil texture, and organic 260 matter content via loss-on-ignition.

- 261 To complement the continuous soil moisture measurements made at discrete locations, and to 262 understand larger-scale variability of moisture patterns, we also measured the soil moisture 263 manually along selected rows and transects at the sites. For this purpose, we used handheld 264 Campbell Scientific Hydrosense II probes. For these measurements, we selected two rows in solar 265 farm 1 (one row upslope and one row downslope) with a length of 85 m, and one row in solar farm 266 2 with length of 92 m, where the selected row was in the vicinity of the soil moisture sensor 267 clusters. For the solar farm 1 measurements, one of the rows is located upslope of the soil moisture 268 cluster, while the second row is located at the same row which we added the sensor cluster (Figure 269 1). Measurements were conducted at 1-2 m intervals along each row. For each row, measurements 270 were conducted at the three key locations relative to the panels: interspace, underpanel and 271 dripline. These manual measurements were made on four selected dates throughout the year that 272 represented a range of hydrologic conditions.

- 273 An additional set of manual soil moisture data was collected to investigate the soil moisture 274 patterns in fine scale with respect to the panels. The first type of manual fine scale measurements 275 was conducted to check if the patterns in the three key locations are consistent. For this purpose, 276 we considered four blocks (1m x 1m) under a panel, four blocks (1m x 1m) in the interspace and 277 four blocks in the dripline (Figure S1).  In the underpanel and interspace blocks, we conducted 278 nine soil moisture measurements and in each dripline block, we made three soil moisture 279 measurements. We conducted one set of these fine-scale measurements for solar farm 1, and one 280 set for solar farm 2.

- 281 In a second series of fine-scale measurements, we surveyed the soil moisture patterns around the 282 dripline (Figure S2). The dripline is one of the locations which is focused on by different 283 researchers when doing soil moisture related measurements in solar farms and is likely a critical 284 area of runoff generation. Therefore, fine scale investigation of soil moisture around the dripline 285 is crucial. In this approach, we considered three lines around the dripline- one line exactly under 286 the dripline, a second line 0.3 m toward the interspace and a third line 0.3 m toward the interspace. 287 We conducted these measurements along the solar panel rows. We conducted this type of 288 measurement at both solar farms.

- 289 Basic vegetation characteristics were also surveyed near the soil moisture sensor clusters at both 290 solar farms. Two-meter plastic quadrats were used at three locations in the underpanel, interspace, 291 and reference zones. For underpanel and interspace, we gathered data in four locations along the

292 panels. For the reference, we randomly selected four locations around the reference location which 293 are not affected by panels. The dripline was not surveyed because its width is narrower than the 294 quadrat. In each quadrat, percent coverage of vegetation by species, bare soil, or rock were noted, 295 as well as maximum height of each species.

296

- 297 2.4. Data Analysis

- 298 For soil moisture time series data, initial quality control was performed where moisture values 299 were removed where soil temperatures were recorded as below freezing. Statistical analysis was 300 conducted using R Statistical Computing Software, version 4.3.1, and graphical evaluation was 301 carried out with Tableau. For manual soil moisture measurements at each solar farm and each date, 302 we employed a Kruskal-Wallis test. When the test statistic was significant, indicating variations 303 among the groups, we conducted post-hoc comparisons to pinpoint the groups with significant 304 differences. Due to a relatively limited number of samples per site for selected soil and vegetation 305 properties, statistical analysis was not conducted on these parameters.

- 306 To assess variations in soil moisture saturation times across different locations, we used soil 307 moisture time series for saturation time comparisons. We conducted two distinct types of 308 saturation time comparisons, leveraging Tableau. The first set of calculations revolved around 309 comparing saturation times at key locations: dripline, underpanel, interspace, reference. We 310 conducted this type of calculation from June to September 2022. The second comparison entailed 311 assessing saturation times at solar farm 2 both before and after the location of the infiltration 312 trench. For this type of analysis, we considered the period of September and October 2022 (note 313 that a different period was used for the trench analysis due to some missing data during summer 314 2022). For these saturation time comparisons, our approach began by identifying the maximum 315 volumetric soil moisture content at each solar farm and each key location (e.g. interspace). 316 Subsequently, we identified the periods during which the soil moisture content remained at its 317 maximum level. We also calculated key summary statistics (e.g. mean, standard deviation) for a 318 year-long period of soil moisture for each sensor location. To characterize variability of soil 319 moisture, we used coefficient of variation, but also adapted the flashiness metric commonly used 320 in streamflow analysis (Baker et al., 2004).

321

323

- 324 This proposed flashiness index (Equation 1) can provide different insight than coefficient of 325 variation. This is because the point-to-point variability characterized by flashiness can differ from 326 the overall variance over a certain time period, relative to the mean, that is characterized by 327 coefficient of variation.

- 328 For the water depth calculations in the infiltration basin of solar farm 1, considerable noise in the 329 data was observed around low/baseline values. To address this, we applied a de-noising technique

- 330 using the moving average method in Tableau. Our findings were then presented in the form of 331 daily rain data versus maximum water depth in the infiltration trench comparison.

## 333 **3. Results and Discussion**

- 334 3.1 Vegetation and soil properties

- 335 A summary of some soil properties and vegetation height are demonstrated in Table 1. Similar to 336 the results of research in solar farms in France, bulk density does not show any specific patterns 337 across the measured key locations (Lambert et al., 2021). In both solar farms, the height of 338 vegetation was higher in the interspace and lower under the panels (Table 1). Vegetation height in 339 the interspace was similar to the reference locations, and even taller in some instances. There was 340 also good coverage of vegetation in the entire solar farm. Areas of rock or bare soil were limited 341 to less than 5%; however, in the underpanel area, there was more dead vegetation (i.e. duff) than 342 in other areas- over a third of the area at solar farm 1. The duff still provides benefits of soil cover 343 like erosion protection. These vegetation characteristics were consistent with research on solar 344 farms in the United Kingdom, which documented taller grasses in the interspace (Armstrong et al., 345 2016). In a Colorado, USA solar farm, there was also greater aboveground plant biomass in the 346 interspace, but underpanel biomass was less than 25% lower (Kannenberg et al., 2023). At solar 347 farm 2, organic matter was higher at the reference in comparison to the other locations. However, 348 at solar farm 1, there was no noticeable difference between the organic matter content of the 349 different locations, similar to the results of the research on UK solar farms which did not show any 350 significant differences in soil physical properties, as compared to a reference location (Armstrong 351 et al., 2016).

356 3.2 Evapotranspiration

357 At both solar farms, we documented consistent differences in solar radiation (Figure S3) and 358 potential ET (PET) (Figure 3) between the under panel and reference locations (Table S3 and Table 359 S4). At solar farm 1, the under panel solar radiation was 87% lower than reference in summer, 360 while in winter it was 60% lower. In solar farm 2, the under panel solar radiation was lower than 361 the reference by 88% in summer and 87% in winter. Despite these similar magnitudes of difference 362 across seasons, there is an overall trend of both the reference and under panel locations to have 363 substantially reduced ET in winter months. The differences across parts of the solar farm align 364 with observations at solar farms in France where lower solar radiation was noticed under panel in 365 comparison to the reference location (Marrou, Dufour, et al., 2013).

366 Calculated PET at the reference location was consistently higher than under the solar panels 367 (Figure 3). In solar farm 1, under panel PET is lower than the reference by 67% in summer and 368 only 1% winter. At solar farm 2, under panel PET is lower than the reference by 37% in summer, 369 while there was no difference in under panel and reference PET in winter. 379 3.3. Continuous soil moisture patterns

380 Various factors, including precipitation, evapotranspiration, and soil or geological features, exert 381 influence over soil moisture patterns within solar farms. Over the course of a year, average 382 volumetric water content at solar farm 1 was 0.33, 0.28, 0.27 and 0.20 for dripline, reference, 383 interspace and underpanel, respectively (Table 2). For solar farm 2, the average VWC was 0.36, 384 0.35, 0.29, and 0.23 for interspace, dripline, reference and underpanel, respectively. At solar farm 385 1, the annual average soil moisture of the dripline is 18% higher than the reference, while the 386 underpanel contains 29% lower soil moisture than the reference. For solar farm 2, average soil 387 moisture at the dripline is 21% higher than the reference, while average underpanel soil moisture 388 is 20% lower than the reference. Thus, the dripline area often exhibits high volumetric water 389 content (VWC), while the underpanel area is relatively drier. Average annual interspace soil 390 moisture is similar to average soil moisture at the reference site at solar farm 1, but is 23% higher 391 than the reference over the course of the year at solar farm 2. Thus soil moisture at the reference 392 locations and interspace areas are often similar, with the interspace at solar farm 2 periodically 393 being wetter. Both the reference and interspace locations are directly impacted by both 394 evapotranspiration and interception of precipitation. The wetter conditions at the solar farm 2 395 interspace may be due to more shading and less ET relative to the reference; unfortunately, solar 396 radiation was not directly measured in the interspace in this study.

The underpanel area does 415 consistently have a lower coefficient of variation than the reference (Table 2). During some dry 416 periods of the summer, the soil moisture of interspace and reference locations gets lower than 417 underpanel, while underpanel soil moisture remains relatively constant, due to more limited ET. 418 For example, during July and August 2022, soil moisture of the interspace at solar farm 1 gets 419 lower than under the panel and at solar farm 2, the reference soil moisture is lower than the 420 underpanel (Figure 4). Research in solar farms in more arid regions (Barron-Gafford et al., 2019; 421 Yue et al., 2021), shows similar results to these summer patterns at these sites, with the underpanel 422 zone often having higher soil moisture. Consequently, in more arid climates, the increased soil 423 moisture under the panels area could be beneficial for plant growth by reducing water limitation. 424 In the winter months, there is an increase in the underpanel soil moisture. In general, soil moisture 425 patterns are more similar between locations in winter, likely due to the more similar ET patterns 426 between the interspace or reference areas and under panel zones in winter months.

- 427 To determine the soil moisture saturation time, we examined soil moisture patterns from June 1, 428 2022, to September 1, 2022, in both solar farms. In this period, at solar farm 1, there was a total of 429 205 minutes when the dripline remained at saturation. In this same period, no saturation was 430 detected in the underpanel and interspace areas, but there were 10 minutes of saturation at the 431 reference location. At solar farm 2, the dripline remained at saturation for a total of 130 minutes. 432 The interspace remained saturated for a total of 15 minutes. No soil saturation was detected under 433 the panel and reference locations. Thus, there is clearly a much longer period of time in which the 434 dripline may be generating runoff, and very limited or no time in which the other areas are likely 435 to be generating runoff.

- 436 3.4. Spatial soil moisture variability in the solar farms

- 437 Manual soil moisture measurements made along entire solar panel rows demonstrate similar 438 patterns to those from the continuous sensors (Figure 5a & b). In the upslope row of solar farm 1 439 on all dates, there were significant differences between the dripline, under panel and interspace 440 (Table S1). On all measurement dates, the dripline had highest soil moisture, followed by 441 interspace and under panel. In the downslope row of solar farm 1 on all four measurement dates, 442 there were significant differences between the dripline with other locations (Table S1). On three 443 dates, the dripline had higher soil moisture, followed by the interspace and under panel. On Feb 444 23, 2022, the interspace had higher soil moisture followed by the dripline and under panel. The 445 potential explanation may stem from the absence of ET and wet soil conditions due to the presence 446 of snow cover in the days preceding the measurements. At solar farm 2 on all dates, there were 447 significant differences between all measurement locations, and dripline consistently had highest 448 soil moisture. Overall, in 11 out of 12 manual measurement campaigns, the dripline contained 449 higher soil moisture and the under panel had the least soil moisture.

This makes sense, given the 464 slope of the panels and landscape, and the fact that water falling from the dripline would be likely 465 to hit the ground just beyond the panel edge and then run downslope. These major changes in 466 moisture occurring over a total of 0.6 m indicate the importance of accurately considering this 467 zone in field and modeling investigation of solar farms.

468 3.5 Function of stormwater management practices

469 Comparison of precipitation data and water level in the infiltration basin at solar farm 1 indicates 470 multiple occurrences of runoff generation and conveyance to the infiltration basin (Figure 6). We 471 evaluated the data over 247 days, in which time there were 84 rain events. The rain events are 472 calculated as the accumulated daily rain. There were 55 rain events that led to maximum daily 473 water level of more than 10 mm in the center of the infiltration basin. The maximum daily rainfall 474 was 67.2 mm, which was less than the 2 year, 24 hour design event of 69 mm. The maximum water 475 level in the infiltration basin during this period was 110 mm and thus never came close to 476 exceeding the actual maximum basin depth of 1 m. Comparison of the water depth in the 477 infiltration basin at the base of solar farm 1 to the dripline saturation patterns indicates some 478 correlation. There is generally some measurable water in the basin, and detectable saturation on 479 days with rain. However, there is not a strong relationship between the magnitude of saturation 480 time and the infiltration basin water level, indicating influence of other factors such as antecedent 481 soil moisture or season (Table S5). It is also important to note that while runoff was detected in 482 the infiltration basin, we cannot conclude whether the runoff captured in the infiltration basin is 483 significantly more than runoff magnitude for comparable storm events prior to solar farm 484 development, due to lack of pre-development monitoring.

- 505 3.6. Implications

- 506 This field investigation shows that there is indeed re-routing of water on solar farms that results in 507 unique, spatially heterogeneous soil moisture patterns. The dripline of the solar panel is clearly the 508 area with highest moisture, and greatest incidence of saturation, and associated potential for runoff 509 reduction. However, we also observe substantial soil moisture reduction from the dripline to the 510 center of the interspace, and minimal occurrence of saturation at the interspace. Frequently, 511 moisture patterns in the interspace are indistinguishable from the reference site; even where 512 average soil moisture is higher in the interspace, there is still little evidence of saturation relative 513 to the dripline. Thus, this interspace disconnection zone between the rows of impervious solar 514 panels is critical. While this study did not directly investigate the impact of vegetation, there was

- 515 high coverage of well-established perennial vegetation at both solar farms, and other work has 516 demonstrated the role that this can play in maintaining soil health, particularly infiltration capacity. 517 Healthy vegetation is also particularly important at the dripline area, in order to minimize the 518 effects of concentrated runoff, and the associated potential for splash erosion. However, some 519 observations point to the need for some engineered structural stormwater management at certain 520 types of sites. These observations include the presence of some differences in soil moisture and 521 saturation patterns between the interspace and reference site, along with reduced incidence of 522 saturation before and after an infiltration trench. The types of landscapes most in need of structural 523 stormwater management are those most prone to runoff generation in undisturbed conditions524 those with steep slopes and poorly draining soils.

- 525 Our research also reveals substantial variations in ET in space and time. These patterns are 526 important for stormwater management, but also for considering the implications for agrivoltaics527 an increasingly popular combination of agriculture (via grazing or cropping) and solar farms. The 528 implications of spatial variation in ET also differs by climatic region. In humid continental regions 529 like where our work was conducted, the underpanel zone had much lower ET than away from solar 530 panels, but this zone was often still drier due to lack of intercepted precipitation. This was reflected 531 in much shorter vegetation, and presence of vegetation is important for managing runoff. In warm 532 arid regions which have much higher solar radiation and reference ET, shading of under panel 533 areas and associated ET reduction can facilitate higher crop production (Barron-Gafford et al., 534 2019; Hassanpour Adeh et al., 2018).

535

- 536 3.7. Innovations, Limitations, and Opportunities

- 537 There is a dearth of work understanding the changes in hydrology on solar farms. Though there 538 has been some investigation of soil moisture changes (Choi et al., 2023), no previously published 539 work to our knowledge has focused on saturation timing and associated potential for runoff 540 generation, or directly evaluated function of stormwater management practices on solar farms. The 541 only existing field research (to our knowledge) directly evaluating runoff quantity and erosion was 542 focused on a limited set of scenarios on bare soils (Wang & Gao, 2023). This type of first-hand 543 measurement is critical as we understand how to best implement and manage solar farms.  It is 544 also important for this work to occur across a range of landscapes. While many solar farms are 545 implemented in landscapes with lower slopes and better draining soils, it is more marginal types 546 of landscapes- some of which were focused on in this work- that need further consideration. As 547 solar farms expand and there is increasing pressure on the most arable and ideal lands, it will be 548 important to understand how to appropriately implement solar farms on marginal lands, with 549 minimal impact on the landscape.

- 550 While field measurements are important for capturing the true response of hydrologic systems, we 551 are still limited in some of the insights we can derive. This and other field data can be used to 552 generate further insight through use in modeling scenarios. Solar farms present a unique landscape 553 transition, and it is important to determine how to best represent the hydrologic changes in 554 modeling programs, particularly to inform stormwater management considerations in the 555 development process (Nair et al., 2023). In this work, it is clear that different parts of the landscape 556 have different potential for runoff generation. Fine-scale soil moisture measurements around the

- 557 dripline also indicate the importance of accurately representing this zone at which precipitation is 558 concentrated.

- 559 This work demonstrated the need for stormwater management considerations on solar farms, 560 particularly those in more runoff-prone landscapes like high slopes. In the two examined solar 561 farms, two different types of structural practices were used (infiltration basins and trenches), in 562 addition to low impact development approaches of impervious disconnection. However, previous 563 review of guidelines for stormwater management on solar farms demonstrates many 564 inconsistencies and variability in solar-specific stormwater management guidance (Yavari et al., 565 2022). Additional field evaluation combined with further development of hydrologic models 566 customized for solar farms can help determine the best way of representing the unique semi567 impervious nature of solar farms along with the appropriate options and sizing of stormwater 568 management strategies.

- 569 It is clear that there are many opportunities and needs for additional field and modeling research 570 on solar farms. While this work introduced some new insights in potential for runoff generation 571 on solar farms, there is still a need for direct measurements of runoff on various parts of solar 572 farms, and at catchment outlets. In many cases, such measurements can be very challenging, 573 depending on the management of the landscape (i.e. avoiding regular mowing that can destroy 574 monitoring setups), and identifying sites where topography facilitates such measurements. 575 Additionally, there is a need to make pre-development measurements in advance of solar farm 576 implementation, rather than relying on space-for-time substitutions (i.e. using a reference location 577 in another nearby location, which may not be a perfect reference).

- 578 **4. Conclusions**

- 579 The rising adoption of solar energy as a renewable resource underscores the importance of assuring 580 that it is being implemented in the most sustainable way. Solar panels introduce impervious 581 surfaces to the landscape and alter land use in their ground-mounted form, highlighting the 582 necessity for effective stormwater management within solar farms. Ground-mounted solar panels 583 differ from conventional impervious surfaces due to the permeable nature of the underpanel area. 584 To prevent adverse environmental outcomes such as erosion and runoff, but to also prevent 585 overestimation of the size and cost of stormwater management practices, thorough and accurate 586 assessment of the landscape impacts of ground-mounted solar panels is essential.

- 587 This work provided new insights on the hydrological phenomena on solar farms, through first588 hand field measurements. It provides some of the first interpretation of saturation and runoff 589 potential on solar farms, in particular on steep and complex landscapes, and the first assessment 590 of structural stormwater management practices on solar farms. While our observations document 591 clear alteration in natural hydrologic patterns, they also demonstrate that adequately sized 592 vegetated spaces between solar panel rows, and in some cases, structural stormwater management, 593 can manage these changes. These types of insights, along with investigation of how land 594 management on solar farms can affect other ecosystem services, can allow us to facilitate this 595 critical transition to renewable energy with minimal ecosystem impact.

## 732 **Abstract**

- 733 As solar energy becomes a cheap source of renewable energy, the number of major utility-scale 734 ground solar panel installations, often called ‘solar farms,’ are growing. With these solar farms 735 often covering hundreds of acres, there is potential for impacts on natural hydrologic processes, 736 including runoff generation and erosion. There is still limited research in this area, and best 737 management practices to address these impacts are variable and not well understood. To fill this 738 gap, we conducted a field investigation of soil moisture patterns, solar radiation, and vegetation 739 at two solar farms in central Pennsylvania, USA that are representative of the complex terrain in 740 the region (e.g., high or variable slopes). Both solar farms also included engineered infiltration 741 basins or trenches that were investigated. Analysis of soil moisture patterns reveals redistribution 742 of water relative to panels, with dripline soil moisture 19% higher than the reference, and 743 underpanel moisture 25% lower than the reference, on average at both solar farms over a year. 744 There are also the greatest periods of saturation and runoff generation at the panel driplines. 745 However, an open interspace between panel rows and existing infiltration basins and trenches are 746 playing a critical role in managing runoff. Micrometeorological monitoring indicates reduced 747 evapotranspiration (ET) under panels, with potential underpanel ET 37-67% lower in summer, 748 and minimal difference in winter. However, a survey of vegetation revealed almost complete 749 ground coverage under panels, which is critical for supporting infiltration and reducing erosion. 750 As solar farms expand to meet important renewable energy goals, it is essential that care be taken 751 to design the landscape to minimize runoff generation and erosion.  This work demonstrates that

- 752 healthy vegetation and well-draining soils can help manage runoff on solar farms; where 753 necessary on more challenging landscapes, engineered stormwater controls can manage any 754 unmitigated runoff.

## 757 **Highlights:**

- 758 • 20-29% lower soil moisture and 60-88% lower solar radiation occurred under panels.

- 759 • There is increased soil moisture and incidence of saturation at the dripline.

- 760 • Differences in ET and soil moisture within the solar farm vary by season.

- 761 • The interspace zone facilitates infiltration, leading to reduced incidence of saturation.

- 762 • Stormwater management strategies can manage changes in runoff from solar farms.
